# Awesome Jev

Independent community project, not affiliated with TypeSafe AI.
Canonical website: https://awesomejev.github.io/
Curated snapshot: 2026-10-17. Findings are author-reported; no model experiments reproduced here.

# Jev guide: typed decisions, probabilities, and evaluation

Jev is a useful case study in models that return decisions for software. This independent guide separates documented interfaces, provider claims, and empirical evaluation. It does not reproduce model experiments.

## What is Jev?

Jev is TypeSafe’s System One model. A request supplies state and typed questions; the response contains bounded answers and probabilities that application code can use for classification, routing, or review. [TypeSafe introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction)

TypeSafe describes its training as reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, or RLCD. That description is a provider claim, not enough information to reconstruct Jev’s architecture or training procedure. [TypeSafe launch article](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev)

## How does a typed decision differ from an LLM’s structured output?

A typed decision interface specifies the permitted alternatives before inference. Generative LLMs can also use constrained decoding to produce structured outputs. An interface alone does not establish which model is more accurate, calibrated, or efficient. [XGrammar paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15100)

A valid answer can still select the wrong option. Keep schema validity separate from semantic correctness, and test ambiguous instructions, adversarial inputs, and option-order changes on your own workload. [Jev 1.13 limitations](https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13)

## What do Choice, Score, and Noul return?

Choice selects from caller-defined options and returns the selected option, a probability for every option, and confidence. Use it for a bounded category or action. [Choice documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice)

Score evaluates ordered, descriptive levels. Its score is the probability-weighted mean of level indices, accompanied by the distribution and confidence; it is not an exact measurement extracted from the input. [Score documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score)

Noul returns the probability that a yes/no proposition is true. It has no separate confidence field. A value near the middle signals uncertainty, not necessarily a medium degree of the property. [Noul documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul)

Keep ordinal label usage, a Score mean, returned confidence, and probability calibration separate. In the tested models and datasets, the v2 ordinal-scale study reports concentrated final choices despite broad average candidate probabilities; finer scales increased compression, and accuracy gains did not necessarily restore utilization. Where a final label is selected, compare its frequency with reference-label frequencies; do not assume every level should occur equally often. Treat this as an additional diagnostic, not a calibration test. The findings are author-reported in the abstract, not our reproduction or evidence that Jev’s Score API has the same failure. [Ordinal-scale utilization study, v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38827v2)

## Is confidence the probability that an answer is correct?

Not automatically. TypeSafe derives confidence from the returned distribution. For Choice, four options with a highest probability of 0.70 produce confidence 0.60. Score uses a different formula. Calibration concerns observed frequencies across predictions, not a guarantee about one answer. [Confidence documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence)

## How should I evaluate decisions and calibration?

Separate prediction quality from probability quality. Alongside accuracy or a task-appropriate error measure, inspect reliability plots and proper scoring rules such as Brier score and log loss. Evaluate on held-out data; do not tune thresholds on the final test set. [Calibration research](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html) · [Proper scoring rules](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/people/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf)

For abstention or escalation, report coverage and error among accepted cases, and test whether the fallback actually corrects mistakes. Freeze model versions and prompts; measure end-to-end latency, failures, and costs separately. This is an evaluation plan, not a result reported for Jev. [SelectiveNet](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/geifman19a.html) · [Model versions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models)

AudioJev uses order calibration to mean probability stability under equivalent candidate permutations. Align candidates by meaning before comparing reordered distributions, then assess accuracy and correctness calibration separately. Its released model card describes one seed, reports original-order scores and discloses audio-source overlap; those results should not be substituted for the paper’s three-seed averages. [AudioJev release scope](https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev)

## How should I compare decision models with trained classifiers and LLMs?

The v2 decision-gate benchmark reports that a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-large had the highest observed accuracy on all but one labeled benchmark. That result concerns access to task labels. For your comparison, separate settings with and without task-specific training labels; record data exposure, development/test splits, output formats and failures before comparing accuracy, selective coverage or cost. [Decision-gate benchmark, v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00346v2)

LLM-as-Jev v3 studies frozen Qwen readouts, optional KL-anchored fine-tuning and budgeted reasoning. To distinguish these effects, we recommend a frozen comparator with the same backbone, explicit option sets and splits, and separately recorded reasoning budgets. The reported comparisons concern two Qwen backbones and an independent framework; they do not reveal hosted Jev’s training or architecture. [LLM-as-Jev, v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02076v3)

HakemBench v1 states that most Turkish reference labels are AI-derived, not human-verified, and that earlier test results influenced the lab’s own model on flagged tracks. Report label provenance, known prior test exposure and per-track metric components. Translation probes should remain separate from independent language validation. These are proposed comparison checks; this collection has not reproduced the studies. [HakemBench, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02293v1)

## Can I reuse a confidence gate across languages or domains?

Before reusing a confidence gate in a new language or domain, build a target-specific test set with explicit label definitions and annotation provenance; translated or model-generated labels are not independent human validation. Compare the unchanged gate with a threshold tuned only on separate target-domain validation data. Report accepted-case error and coverage per group, including high-confidence errors under independently checked, answer-preserving context additions.

The social-science audit reports task-dependent confidence failures using benchmark labels; JevOut’s human checks cover only sampled successful perturbations. Neither abstract establishes multilingual transfer. Language-specific label checks and threshold-transfer comparisons are our proposed protocol, not reproduced findings or population-wide guarantees. [Social-science annotation audit, v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24574v2) · [JevOut, v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30243v2)

Implementation documentation supplies additional transfer limits. FRIDA-Decisions recommends short Russian–English states and uses Russian instruction suffixes. Jev-AR reports synthetic Arabic training without native-speaker validation and says confidence fitted to its built-in routes is approximate on custom lists. These are documented operating conditions, not evidence that a confidence gate transfers; we did not run either implementation. [FRIDA-Decisions limits](https://github.com/ai-forever/frida-decisions) · [Jev-AR limitations](https://github.com/atmaneayoubdev/jev-ar)

The Indonesian regional-language study supplies a concrete separation: expected calibration error did not increase while error-ranking ability degraded. Its translation comparison uses human Indonesian translations; classifier comparisons depend on label budgets, and cascades on the chosen fallback and routing fraction. Evaluate those factors separately before transferring a threshold. The preregistration and release claims remain author-reported here; no prediction files were audited. [Indonesian regional-language transfer study, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14112v1)

## How should I test decisions over tables and cited evidence?

Separate schema validity, stability under content-preserving changes, and semantic correctness against reference labels. For tables, pair original inputs with alternative layouts or row/column reorderings only when meaning is preserved. Keep values, relationships and arithmetic fixed, then compare choices and probability distributions. A stable answer can still be wrong; low confidence alone does not identify an error. [Tabular decision preprint, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19536v1)

For citations, keep the claim and arithmetic fixed while swapping same-number passages that support a different financial role. Include equivalent valid evidence as positive controls, and measure false acceptance of mismatches and false rejection of valid support separately. Inspect paired disagreements rather than counting every changed answer as wrong. These constructed cases are diagnostic probes, not estimates of error rates in real traffic. [Same-number citation preprint, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08675v1)

## How should I test tool arguments and option-channel risks?

Separate schema validity, whether cited evidence supports a proposed argument, and whether the argument follows from the request, history and schema defaults. Test correct defaults or inferred values without explicit references, alongside incorrect values paired with visible references. Reference availability is not derivation correctness. If a model writes references from the full history, hide the candidate from it and verify its output; generated references are not ground truth. [Tool-argument verification preprint, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18497v1)

Define who can alter request text, tool outputs, option names and policy definitions. Test each channel your threat model lets an attacker control, including confidence on incorrect decisions. The cited guardrail experiments concern open-weight typed-decision models, not a demonstrated compromise of hosted Jev. This is a proposed evaluation protocol, not a reproduced result. [Option-channel guardrail preprint, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292v1)

Separate evidence of label sensitivity from its mechanism. In the open implementations studied by Labels Override Definitions, changing label/definition rendering while holding weights fixed changed the bias. For a system you can inspect, record the rendered request and compare conflicting labels with definition-only or neutral-label variants. This is a proposed diagnostic; it neither identifies hosted Jev’s internal mechanism nor establishes a universal defense. [Labels Override Definitions, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586v1)

## What does an attack success rate measure?

Define the outcome and denominator before calling an attack successful. Probability shifts, action changes, attacker-target selections and downstream harm are different outcomes. Same Attack measures pass-after-attack only among malicious cases each judge flagged when clean. Its separate Jev gate-bypass measure requires a less restrictive action with returned confidence for the severity Score ≥0.7; review can qualify, while low-confidence pass need not. [Same Attack metric definitions, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.17820v1#S4.SS5)

Compare attacks with matched unchanged requests using the same decision rule. JevAdvBench distinguishes a changed most-likely Score level from a changed expected score. For adaptive search, separate optimization calls from validation: Decision Hijacking freezes candidates, then uses five fresh calls and requires at least three target selections for case-level success. This finite-repeat rule does not guarantee later success. [JevAdvBench typed metrics, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.31142v1#S1.p4.1) · [Decision Hijacking validation, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.28613v1#S4.SS4)

Decision Hijacking reports 51 target selections in 2,550 calls for one condition, but 11 majority-success cases out of 510: the denominators answer different questions. Same Attack reports 75% raw severity changes on repeated Jev moderation calls but only 1% routed-action changes. These are author-reported examples, not reproduced results or a ranking. Check answer preservation and delivery separately; equal token counts alone do not prove that an edit was removed. [Call-level and case-level counts, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.28613v1#A1.SS4.p2.1) · [Raw versus routed instability, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.17820v1#A2) · [Delivery inference limits, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.31142v1#S3.SS3.p3.1)

## Are the SDK and independent models released Jev weights?

The official SDK is a client for TypeSafe’s hosted API, not a Jev checkpoint. Independent projects such as Laya publish their own model artifacts. Similar question types or API compatibility do not establish identical architecture, behavior, or accuracy. [Official Python SDK](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python) · [Laya model card](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya)

Check each release’s model card and license separately. For example, Bespoke Nimble 9B v3 declares CC BY-NC 4.0, which restricts commercial use. Publicly downloadable artifacts should not all be labeled unrestricted open-source models. [Bespoke Nimble v3 model card](https://huggingface.co/bespokelabs/Bespoke-Nimble-9B-v3)

API shape does not determine the inference path. Span-02 documents its own runtime and optional generated reasoning, with index settings that differ from normal serving. Lychee documents rejection rather than truncation for oversized requests. Record engine, hardware, reasoning mode, confidence definition and input limits with a comparison; these are publisher descriptions, not deployments tested by this collection. [Span-02 runtime and index settings](https://huggingface.co/respanai/span-02/raw/63cbdd774391f1b7d9bc3829179efe996d0191ce/README.md) · [Lychee model-card limits](https://huggingface.co/LycheeAI/Lychee-27B/raw/f3f95d18a3b1ef3c483c2a5d7e8e5272a2af31e2/README.md)

## Where should I look for research and benchmark evidence?

Start with versioned empirical papers and their available code or data. The broad Jev benchmark study is one entry point; its findings remain author-reported, rather than independently reproduced by this collection. [Jev benchmark paper, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37647v1) · [Accompanying benchmark code](https://github.com/AppliedMachineLearning-Lab/jev-benchmarking)

TypeSafe WorkflowEvals publishes workflows and model-generated reference labels; agreement with those references differs from human-label accuracy. The community Decision Index also contains private tests, so public rankings do not make the entire evaluation independently reproducible. The reviewed 0.3.2 snapshot uses a Jev 1.14 lab reference, while its frozen request payloads still name Jev 1.13. Record the model that produced a result separately from the model named in archived inputs. [WorkflowEvals](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/WorkflowEvals) · [Decision Index methodology snapshot](https://huggingface.co/spaces/multimodalart/jev-decision-index/blob/0ddf6758073eb77ae449a3541f57286d7f39d93f/data/methodology.json)

Model cards may describe different evaluation conditions within one table. KnowLine discloses checkpoint selection using public-suite scores and task/source overlap in training. Amos separates zero-shot results from a setting that fits question priors on the benchmark’s train split. Keep those conditions separate, and do not treat publisher-run public results as the private-inclusive Decision Index score or as our reproduction. [KnowLine selection and disclosures](https://huggingface.co/PelaAI/KnowLine-35B-A3B-Gen1/raw/e800968d38761c190476da5c69c6a5087a3c9b29/README.md) · [Amos evaluation conditions](https://huggingface.co/mukaddamzaid/amos-1-large/raw/d67e051c763dc88a1e3662a5003c1e1ea5ffaa74/README.md)

## What can I reproduce from a public research artifact?

Name what you want to reproduce: tables or plots from scored summaries, metrics from released per-example answers, fresh predictions, or a trained checkpoint. Map each output to its required inputs, versions and hashes. Report whether materials were only inspected, commands were executed, or outputs were matched; these are different claims.

Visual Jev’s pinned reproduction guide describes regenerating specified tables and two plots from scored JSON without a GPU. Other figures need omitted per-example predictions and intervention analyses. Fresh predictions require upstream corpora, backbone weights and a GPU; source images are not redistributed. [Visual Jev reproduction guide, pinned commit](https://github.com/guanxuyu-sv/Visual-Jev/blob/a392eaedfa41adae348f9767b55c0f54b3a13b57/REPRODUCE.md)

The observed ordinal-scale artifact documents metric recomputation from released answers. Fresh inference is separate: source text, weights and post-trained checkpoints are omitted, and missing historical data revisions can prevent a reconstruction matching recorded hashes. Its opaque file revision is not an immutable Git commit. Preserve mismatches rather than silently substituting current data. [Ordinal-scale study, v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38827v2) · [Observed anonymous README, opaque file revision](https://anonymous.4open.science/api/repo/jev_ordinal_scale_bia/file/README.md?v=3ed72968)

The radiology paper’s v1 availability statement says analysis scripts and aggregate results are being prepared for release. Third-party dataset links do not supply those missing author outputs. Our checks concern documentation and selected file inventories; we have not executed these reproduction routes or independently reproduced their results. [Radiology availability statement, v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.27607v1#Sx1.p1)

For control loops, a replay of isolated model latency does not establish deadline attainment. The network-control SoK separates request queues, execution times, action feasibility and responsibility for service checks; its examples use one bounded event model. Our proposed deployment check records arrival patterns and the complete path from request to verified outcome, alongside misses and infeasible actions. It does not substitute a synthetic replay for production evidence. [Semantic decision engines in network control, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06425v1)

# Curated resources

## Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions

Papers · Fang et al. · 2026-10-15 · v1

An independent Jev-style decision head on Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next gives Choice, Noul and Score readouts over audio, reporting 84.06% on MMSU, a 6.50% speaker-verification equal error rate and about 20× faster inference than its own base model.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21614v1

## JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs

Papers · Zhu et al. · 2026-10-15 · v1

Studies fitted confidence thresholds for sharing agent control with decision models.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21412v1

## System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?

Papers · Chen et al. · 2026-10-15 · v1

A benchmark spanning matched requests and closed-loop tasks. Experiments have not been reproduced here.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21244v1

## Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences

Papers · Deng, Fan, Zhang & Xie · 2026-10-15 · v3

In ten prepared scientific cases, the authors separate semantic selections, computed quantities and final labels; comparison-model errors can be hidden by unchanged final labels.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24965v3

## From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection

Papers · Lan, Kaul, Pandurangan & Sanyal · 2026-10-14 · v1

On 47,611 held-out prompt-injection examples, Jev ranks second in AUROC after an LLM judge, its native probabilities do not consistently beat post-hoc calibrated classifiers, and a 1% false-negative target forces over 91.8% escalation in every gate-reviewer system.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20907v1

## Calibration and Risk-Budgeted Decisions with System One Models

Papers · Messoudi & Mansar · 2026-10-14 · v1

Jev and other System One models make binary allow/block or retain/discard decisions without human deferral; across six moderation, safety and reranking datasets, naive threshold selection exceeds the target risk in about half the settings, against 7.8% for Learn Then Test.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19811v1

## Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop

Papers · Zheng & Chen · 2026-10-14 · v1

Gates reasoning start, candidate-answer reading and generation stopping; evidence is limited to a frozen Qwen backbone and three task families.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19644v1

## Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev

Papers · Imperatrice, Kameneva, Greenberg & Romano · 2026-10-14 · v1

In 41,500 responses Jev's selected answers look largely unbiased, but its judgments shift with irrelevant numbers and option order, and several bias manipulations move its probabilities even when the answer stays the same; on 30 adapted conjunction tasks it violates the conjunction rule in 54% of 15,000 responses.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19619v1

## Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data

Papers · Zhang, Ye & Zha · 2026-10-14 · v1

Tests classification and verification under content-preserving table rewrites across three task families; confidence can flag instability without proving correctness.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19536v1

## More Choices, Fewer Decisions: Ordinal-Scale Bias in JEV-like Direct-Decision Models

Papers · Gao et al. · 2026-10-14 · v2

Audits ordinal label underuse across selected decision models; finer scales increase compression, while accuracy, final-label utilization and averaged candidate probabilities remain distinct measures.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38827v2

## DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision

Papers · Lan et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

Text and vision attacks with label-validity checks and held-out evaluation models.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19118v1

## Jeva: System One Models from First Principles

Papers · Li & Wang · 2026-10-13 · v1

A decision-model architecture exploring null handling, option permutations, scaling, and caching. Its design is Jeva’s, not Jev’s disclosed internals.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18773v1

## VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction

Papers · Zhu et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

Structured video decisions with temporal spans and candidate scores; cached and joint inference reuse visual computation.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18615v1

## Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications

Papers · Luo et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

JevProbe traces attacker-controlled context into the decisions that 228 popular Jev applications act on; in 2,273 curated cases (at most ten per app, flips selected first, so not an unbiased sample) 81.5% flip, 98.6% of flips with potential downstream security impact, and existing defenses offer limited protection.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18612v1

## Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models

Papers · Chung et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

On 11,117 English Theory of Mind questions from nine benchmarks, Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy and ranks first or second in all six capability groups among twelve typed and generative models; confidence-based selection is benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons repair or overturn answers depending on how they are attached.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18610v1

## Reading Right, Acting Wrong: Diagnosing Decision Failures of System One Models in Agent Loops

Papers · Li, Krishnan & Padman · 2026-10-13 · v1

Pairs factual probes with action choices to diagnose decision failures.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18579v1

## How Reliable Are System-One Decisions in Medicine? A Comparative Study of Jev, Jev-like Models, and LLMs

Papers · Du et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

Across 15 medical datasets (8,742 instances), Jev rivals leading models on text-driven tasks, is weaker on numerical ones and is the most stable under question-format changes; most models miss absent correct answers. A benchmark study, not clinical validation.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18529v1

## Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments

Papers · Ma et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

Tool-argument judges including Jev reject some correct derived values without visible references; model-generated references are evaluated on three benchmarks.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18497v1

## Same Attack, Different Judge: A First Controlled Adversarial Comparison of Jev, LLM Judges, and Purpose-Built Safety Classifiers

Papers · Li et al. · 2026-10-13 · v1

A controlled adversarial comparison of Jev, LLM judges, and purpose-built safety classifiers.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17820v1

## LLM-as-Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them

Papers · Li & Wagle · 2026-10-13 · v3

Compares frozen Qwen decision readouts with optional KL-anchored fine-tuning and budgeted reasoning; reported gains depend on backbone size and routing workload, not disclosure of hosted Jev internals.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02076v3

## Decision Models vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places

Papers · Rao & Callison-Burch · 2026-10-13 · v3

Compares rubric judges and examines correlated errors that can limit cascade improvements.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29769v3

## Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models

Papers · Geuter, Cheng & Alvarez-Melis · 2026-10-12 · v1

Answer-letter readout and supervised LoRA baselines; evaluation includes model-generated labels.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17205v1

## Does a Hosted Decision Model Respect Irrelevant Alternatives? A Pre-Registered Test of Option-Set Dependence in Jev

Papers · Rajput, Chauhan & Kosaraju · 2026-10-12 · v1

Adding an irrelevant option shifts jev-1.13.0’s gold-versus-rival log-odds, more so as options grow, so its probabilities are relative to the option list; independent yes/no scoring removes this but is less accurate (pre-registered, 299,463 calls, three datasets).

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16655v1

## GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks

Papers · Yang, Zhang & Zhao · 2026-10-12 · v3

Compares graph decisions across fourteen model-interface configurations; local adjacency, graph-text evidence use and sequential solution quality are separate capabilities.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06354v3

## General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev

Papers · Duan et al. · 2026-10-12 · v2

Bilingual decision evaluation and reliability when local decisions compose into larger systems.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03935v2

## Suggested Is Not Superseded: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a System-One Model as a Memory-Retirement Gate

Papers · Chen & Le · 2026-10-11 · v1

Jev memory-retirement evaluation separates confirmed updates from suggestions; mixed LLM/human labels, shared errors and selection on a small development set constrain cascade claims.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15710v1

## SanSi: A Looped Typed Decision Model for System 1.5 Thinking

Papers · Gan, Lee & Kang · 2026-10-10 · v2

Looped hidden-state computation for typed decisions; additional loops trade compute for accuracy.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07730v2

## JevCascade: Readout Stability and Inference-Time Compute Allocation for Prefill-Only Decision Models

Papers · Li & Chen · 2026-10-10 · v2

Candidate-menu interventions and confidence cascades; ranking stability does not establish probability calibration.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07716v2

## Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation

Papers · Madrid-García & Merino-Barbancho · 2026-10-10 · v4

Preliminary medical-benchmark evaluation of Jev 1.13 reports task-dependent accuracy, calibration and weak unanswerable-question detection; it does not establish clinical deployment validity.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34024v4

## Same Scores, Different Decisions: Evaluating JEV and Language Models for Legal Document Understanding

Papers · Zhang et al. · 2026-10-10 · v2

ContractNLI request variations can change which answers are wrong while aggregate accuracy stays unchanged; stable answers may preserve errors. This benchmark does not validate real legal deployment.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27678v2

## Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages

Papers · Fadli et al. · 2026-10-09 · v1

Tests Jev and multilingual Laya on Indonesian regional-language tasks; stable expected calibration error can coexist with worse error ranking, while human translation, label budgets and cascade choices change comparisons.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14112v1

## When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows

Papers · Ling, Yu, Chen & Fang · 2026-10-09 · v1

Jev cut decision cost and latency for five agents in ALFWorld and AndroidWorld (4,500 runs), but two mobile agents lost more success, extra reasoning and interactions absorbed the savings, and cost per success rose for one agent.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13092v1

## TypedBench: A Benchmark for Calibration, Framing Sensitivity, and Cost in System One Decision Models

Papers · Sharma, Duncan, Caron & Vollmer · 2026-10-09 · v2

The hosted model is wording-sensitive and underconfident, and under asymmetric costs acting on its probabilities can cost more than taking its top answer; synthetic policy-labelled suites also report paraphrase ranges and calibration against a finite-sample noise floor.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11392v2

## JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure

Papers · Li et al. · 2026-10-09 · v5

Studies confidence-based escalation from Jev to a reasoning judge, including limits under distribution shift.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26550v5

## One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails

Papers · Azizi, Baghaei Potraghloo & Pedram · 2026-10-08 · v1

Tests option-channel attacks on seven open-weight models; reversed decisions can remain confident. The reported experiments do not test hosted Jev.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292v1

## Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks

Papers · Li et al. · 2026-10-08 · v1

Knowledge, reasoning and multilingual multiple-choice evaluation of Jev; reported rankings and mathematical weaknesses apply to the selected models and benchmarks.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11978v1

## MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface

Papers · Cheng et al. · 2026-10-08 · v1

Bi-encoder approach to multimodal decisions and retrieval through natural-language interfaces.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316v1

## JevOut: Natural Context Can Flip Decision Models

Papers · Xu et al. · 2026-10-08 · v2

Optimizes context additions around unchanged questions and options in four decision systems; results concern initially correct decisions, and human validity checks cover a sampled subset of successful attacks.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30243v2

## Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free: Typed Decision Models Follow the Option Name, Not the Definition Bound to It

Papers · Sun, Xu, Shi & Yang · 2026-10-08 · v3

Tests conflicts between option names and definitions despite structurally valid outputs.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26758v3

## Same-Number Citation Swaps: Stress-Testing Jev as a Financial Evidence Judge

Papers · Xu et al. · 2026-10-06 · v1

Same-number citation swaps probe financial-evidence verification; rejecting wrong roles trades off with accepting equivalent support in a constructed test.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08675v1

## Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via System One-Guided Computational Division of Labor

Papers · Zhou et al. · 2026-10-06 · v1

Separates bounded multi-agent coordination from LLM reasoning through a controller–reader loop; reported GPT-4o-token and end-to-end latency reductions concern complete framework comparisons on seven benchmarks.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08155v1

## JEV versus LLMs: Accuracy, Cost and Calibration on Seven Political Science Replications

Papers · Denney & DiGiuseppe · 2026-10-06 · v2

Studies accuracy, cost, and calibration in seven political-science replication tasks.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06625v2

## Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates

Papers · Rafe & Das · 2026-10-06 · v2

A common-request harness compares typed decision models, generative readouts and trained classifiers; accuracy, selective coverage and out-of-scope acceptance depend on label access and task.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00346v2

## ufakzeka-karar: An Open Turkish Typed-Decision Model with Order-Invariant Option Scoring

Papers · Teke · 2026-10-05 · v1

An open 182M-parameter Turkish model scores each option blind to the others, so answers ignore option order, and adds a “not sure” signal; its 7th-of-16 HakemBench rank is not blind, since later runs trained after full-test results were read.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06744v1

## SoK: Semantic Decision Engines in Network Control Loops

Papers · Li et al. · 2026-10-05 · v1

Surveys semantic engines in network control loops; separates valid decisions, action feasibility, service checks and deadline attainment, with bounded event-model tests rather than production validation.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06425v1

## Hidden Risks of Jev: An Empirical Study of Security, Privacy, and Dual Use

Papers · Wang et al. · 2026-10-04 · v1

Tests the official Jev API and the local NanoJev for prompt injection, data-poisoning backdoors, membership, attribute and knowledge inference, and dual use in four detection tasks; the authors report Jev remains vulnerable to the examined threats.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04985v1

## Calibrated to Whom? Persona and Language Effects on Cultural Values in JEV

Papers · Asseri & Asseri · 2026-10-03 · v2

English/Arabic persona-conditioned Jev survey audit; the effects concern simulated respondents in one model, not measurements of real populations.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36399v2

## Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation

Papers · Liu · 2026-10-03 · v3

Examines reliability, group-specific confident errors, and selective automation in security decisions.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33401v3

## Batched Speech Decisions Without Decoding: Single-Token Supervision Lets a Frozen LLM Hear Beyond the Transcript

Papers · Jin et al. · 2026-10-02 · v1

DuplexJev connects ASR hidden states to a frozen LLM for batched answer-token readout; connector-specific speech tasks and eight-GPU timing do not establish single-device or live-agent latency.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638v1

## Labels Override Definitions in Jev-Style Typed Decision Models

Papers · Azizi, Baghaei Potraghloo & Pedram · 2026-10-01 · v1

Studies option-label bias in open-weight decision models; prompt-rendering changes with fixed weights implicate the label/definition interface, without testing hosted Jev.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586v1

## HakemBench: A Turkish Benchmark of Typed Decisions

Papers · Teke · 2026-10-01 · v1

Turkish typed-decision evaluation reports decision quality, Brier-based probability quality and risk–coverage alongside input probes; most labels are AI-derived, and the lab’s model used feedback from earlier test results.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02293v1

## AudioJev: Direct Audio Decisions with Order-Calibrated Probabilities

Papers · Lv et al. · 2026-10-01 · v1

Learns audio-conditioned candidate probabilities with aligned option-permutation training; order stability and empirical correctness calibration remain different properties.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293v1

## Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model

Controls information and surface cues to distinguish Jev answer confidence from self-knowledge; black-box behavior does not establish access to an internal knowledge state.

## SearchJev training pipeline

Tools · EvoScientist · training code · Apache-2.0

Search-agent decision training with soft-label and Brier losses, reliability weights and per-question-type temperature fitting; the documented pipeline and split controls were not reproduced.

Primary source: https://github.com/evoscientist/searchjev

## mJev

Tools · SoMarkAI · multimodal runtime · Apache-2.0

Shared-context candidate scoring with HF/vLLM routes; normalized option probabilities are not calibrated confidence, and the reported cache speedup trades higher memory in one controlled video setup.

Primary source: https://github.com/somarkai/mjev

## FRIDA-Decisions

Tools · SberAI · independent runtime · MIT code

Packed Russian–English encoder runtime for typed questions and ranking; state truncation, Russian instruction suffixes and margin-versus-probability semantics remain explicit.

## OpenThai-SystemOne

Tools · iapp-technology · Thai/English pipeline

Thai/English text decision-model training and serving pipeline with a slot readout; the documented recipe does not establish independently validated calibration or interface equivalence.

## Quyet runtime

Runtime for Quyet decision models with checkpoint-dependent English/Vietnamese coverage; it documents ten-option limits and state truncation, without evaluated adversarial robustness.

## JevLang

Tools · timmikeladze · policy and replay

TypeScript/Python policy layer separates typed model answers from routing and action dispatch, with documented journals and replay; a trace does not establish truthful inputs or calibrated thresholds.

Primary source: https://github.com/timmikeladze/jevlang

## sysone decision-learning library

# Research topics

## Option-label bias in Jev-style decision models

Canonical page: https://awesomejev.github.io/topics/option-label-bias/
Updated: 2026-10-17

A valid typed answer can follow an option’s familiar name instead of its assigned definition. The observed failure and its cause are separate questions: evidence from inspected open implementations should not be treated as an explanation of hosted Jev’s internals.

Independent research note based on versioned abstracts and the collection’s scoped reviews. Findings are author-reported; no attack or model experiment was run here.

### Which studies answer which question?

Sun and colleagues test conflicts between option names and definitions. Azizi and colleagues’ Labels Override Definitions examines how open implementations render those fields, including interventions that hold weights fixed. Their later One Word Opens the Gate evaluates attacker-controlled option channels in guardrail settings. These are distinct papers with different experimental questions; sharing a failure theme does not make their results interchangeable. [Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free, v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26758v3) · [Labels Override Definitions, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586v1) · [One Word Opens the Gate, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292v1)

### Why inspect the rendered request?

The fixed-weight rendering intervention in Labels Override Definitions provides evidence about the tested interface implementation. That is a narrower claim than saying every constrained decision head has the same defect. Before comparing systems, identify whether the option key, label and definition all reach the model, and whether the adapter rewrites or drops any of them. [Rendering intervention: original abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586v1)

### A diagnostic to use in your own evaluation

Our suggested comparison fixes the state, task rule, model version and scoring rule. Prepare equivalent requests with informative labels, neutral identifiers and definition-only options where the interface permits them. Add a separate conflicting-label condition, with expected answers checked before querying. Compare answer changes, errors and confidence on errors; preserve the actual rendered inputs. Use a held-out set to test any proposed repair.

### What would remain unproven?

An adapter fix on one open implementation is not a universal injection defense. The guardrail study concerns open-weight models and does not demonstrate a compromise of hosted Jev. Keep the attacker’s permitted input channels explicit, and distinguish a changed distribution, a wrong choice and a downstream action. The diagnostic above is a proposed protocol, not a reproduced finding. [Guardrail study and tested scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292v1)

## AudioJev: audio decisions, order calibration and release limits

Canonical page: https://awesomejev.github.io/topics/audiojev/
Updated: 2026-10-17

AudioJev is an independent audio decision model that scores supplied alternatives from a waveform and question. Its order-calibration objective addresses sensitivity to candidate order; it does not establish that a returned probability equals the empirical chance of being correct.

Based on the fixed-v1 abstract, public model card and inference-library overview. No weights, audio or inference code were executed or downloaded.

### What does the model return?

The paper describes training paired candidate orders and aligning their distributions by candidate identity. Inference scores the supplied candidates without an order ensemble. The separate inference library exposes Choice and Noul requests, plus an experimental Score interface, and can share an audio encoding across questions. This is a closed set: your application still has to supply appropriate alternatives and a fallback when needed. [AudioJev paper, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293v1) · [Inference-library documentation](https://github.com/SihanLv/AudioJev-Inference)

### How does DuplexJev differ?

DuplexJev connects ASR-encoder states to a frozen language model, whereas AudioJev describes a shared full-parameter model with an option-order objective. The speech paper reports different connector configurations and timing on an eight-GPU node. These are different training and serving arrangements, not a matched speed comparison. For a useful comparison, hold audio tasks, candidate sets, batching and hardware fixed, and separate audio encoding, question scoring and end-to-end latency. [DuplexJev, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638v1) · [AudioJev, v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293v1)

### Which results belong to the released checkpoint?

Keep the paper’s three-seed averages separate from the model card’s single-seed, original-order results. The card also discloses audio-source overlap in part of the hidden MMAU evaluation. Neither a hidden evaluation split nor a fixed final checkpoint automatically establishes independence from all fitting or development sources. [Checkpoint and evaluation scope](https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev)

### How should I evaluate it?

For your own test, define a task-specific answer set and verify labels independently. Compare unchanged audio under meaning-preserving candidate permutations, align the returned probabilities by candidate identity, and measure both accuracy and order sensitivity. Assess correctness calibration separately, on held-out labeled examples. If a downstream action depends on a threshold, report the accepted fraction and error rate together. These are proposed checks, not results produced by this collection.

### What is available, and under which terms?

The library is presented as Apache-2.0 code; the checkpoint declares the separate Qwen Research license. Review the model’s own terms before use. The release does not establish open-ended generation, visual performance or live turn-taking readiness. Follow the linked runtime documentation for hardware and deployment requirements; a documented command is not a verified deployment by this project. [Model card and license declaration](https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev) · [Runtime and deployment entry point](https://github.com/SihanLv/AudioJev-Inference)

## GraphDecisionBench: evaluating Jev on graph decisions

Canonical page: https://awesomejev.github.io/topics/graph-decision-benchmarks/
Updated: 2026-10-17

GraphDecisionBench evaluates different graph capabilities rather than producing one universal model ranking. Correctly recognizing an edge does not establish structural reasoning, and completing a feasible construction does not establish a high-quality solution.

This note uses the v3 abstract and the repository’s overview and availability statements. It is not a full-paper review or benchmark reproduction.

### What are the three evaluation questions?

The benchmark separates structural graph queries, the use of graph-plus-text information, and decisions that construct a solution over multiple steps. These comparisons diagnose different behavior. Fourteen model-interface configurations appear across the experiments; that count should not be relabeled as fourteen independent models or as identical coverage of every task. [GraphDecisionBench paper, v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06354v3)

### What must be matched before comparing scores?

The repository treats each task and input condition separately and documents unsupported interfaces. Its structural probes use small supplied graphs and constructed answer quotas, which do not represent natural label frequencies in the source networks. When assessing a comparison, inspect the task predicate, candidate set, scoring rule and adapter before drawing a broader capability conclusion. [Task contracts and input conditions](https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench)

### A useful control for sequential decisions

Our suggested evaluation compares a model-driven selector with the proposal rule alone, using the same candidate generator, constraints and stopping conditions. Measure feasibility and final objective quality separately. Preserve unsuccessful trajectories and their costs. If a heuristic narrows the choices, any improvement may reflect both the proposals and the selector; an identical proposal-only control helps separate their contributions.

### Which version and artifacts are covered?

The paper was first submitted on October 5, 2026; this note uses v3 dated October 12. The repository offers code and aggregate tables but states that per-query and per-trajectory outputs are not distributed. Regenerating a chart from summaries would therefore be a different operation from checking individual predictions or rerunning the models. No such operation was performed here. [Versioned paper and submission history](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06354v3) · [Public release scope](https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench)
